summary: Documents a process for organizing future development of SIP and related work in the Real-time Applications and Infrastructure area. It aims to keep changes and extensions coordinated as SIP is used in more environments. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5727 sets out how the IETF handles changes to SIP and related real-time work. It assigns core SIP maintenance to SIPCORE and uses DISPATCH to route other proposals to an appropriate effort.

subtitle: Defines how the IETF organizes core SIP changes and reviews new work in the RAI Area.

tldr.problem: SIP's use in many environments brought proposals for modifications and extensions. The IETF needed a process that protected interoperability while giving new work a clear path.
tldr.mechanism: SIPCORE handles documents changing core SIP specifications, while DISPATCH identifies an appropriate venue for other new work in the Real-time Applications and Infrastructure Area.
tldr.outcome: The RFC replaces the earlier P-header process and obsoletes RFC 3427. It is a Best Current Practice and has been updated by RFC 7957.

today: RFC 5727 is Best Current Practice BCP 67, published in March 2010, and obsoletes RFC 3427. It updates RFC 3265 and RFC 3969, and has been updated by RFC 7957.

sections.title: Why SIP Needed a Change Process
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) grew beyond its initial use for Internet multimedia sessions. As more groups proposed changes, the IETF needed to preserve baseline interoperability across implementations.

RFC 5727 replaces RFC 3427 and describes a new structure for work in the Real-time Applications and Infrastructure (RAI) Area. It assigns long-term responsibilities to two working groups.
sections.plainLanguage: As SIP gained more uses, many groups proposed changes to it. This RFC defines a process for reviewing and organizing that work.

sections.title: Responsibilities of SIPCORE and DISPATCH
sections.content:
SIPCORE handles documents that update or obsolete RFCs 3261 through 3265 or their successors. SIP extensions considered by SIPCORE must be Standards Track.

DISPATCH considers new work across the RAI Area and identifies a suitable venue. It can route a proposal to SIPCORE, an existing effort, or a new group or working group; it can also recommend that work not proceed at that time. A DISPATCH review is not required before a proposed core SIP change goes to SIPCORE.
sections.plainLanguage: SIPCORE handles changes to the core SIP specifications. DISPATCH reviews other new proposals and identifies where they should be considered.

sections.title: Introducing New Work
sections.content:
Proposals are best written as individual Internet-Drafts. The RFC says a problem statement should explain what needs solving, why existing mechanisms are insufficient, why SIP is an appropriate solution when SIP is being changed, and what security issues may result.

When work falls outside existing RAI charters, DISPATCH and the Area Directors decide whether it warrants a new effort. A DISPATCH deliverable can be a problem statement or charter, but must not include protocol development. Once an approved new effort is formed, it becomes autonomous.
sections.plainLanguage: Describe the problem before settling on a protocol change. If existing work does not cover it, DISPATCH helps identify a suitable new effort.

sections.title: Why the P- Header Process Was Deprecated
sections.content:
The former P- header prefix was intended for extensions with limited or private use. The RFC says the prefix did not prevent a popular header from being used more broadly and left no practical path for converting it to general use.

RFC 5727 therefore deprecates the earlier guidance for creating P- headers. Existing P- headers continue to be handled as their specifications say. New informational header fields may be registered under Designated Expert review if they remain informational, do not significantly change SIP behavior, and do not undermine security.
sections.plainLanguage: The P- prefix did not keep a header limited to its original setting. New informational headers instead go through expert review under stated conditions.

sections.title: Reviewing SIP Event Packages
sections.content:
RFC 5727 changes the registration process for normal SIP event packages. A proposal developed outside a chartered IETF working group must first be published as an Internet-Draft for DISPATCH review.

A Designated Expert reviews an outside proposal under the RFC Required policy. It must not define a template package, overlap with chartered packages, contradict SIP behavior, or undermine security. It must be documented in an Informational RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: New event packages are reviewed before registration. The review checks that they fit existing SIP work and do not conflict with its rules or security.

sections.title: Registry Rules and Security Requirements
sections.content:
Method names, option tags, and response codes still require a Standards Action. Informational SIP header fields that do not begin with P- may be registered with Designated Expert approval. The RFC also clarifies that registering new SIP URI parameters requires Standards Action.

New requirements for SIP must discuss security implications. RFCs that modify or extend SIP must address security and feature interactions without worsening SIP's existing security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Different SIP registry entries use different review processes. Every proposed SIP change must also explain its security implications.

items.title: New RAI effort
items.text: A new group or effort is formed for the work.

items.title: Existing work
items.text: The proposal belongs in an existing chartered effort.

items.title: No action now
items.text: The proposal is not pursued at that time.
